meta.name: Brussels Griffon Puppy Checklist
meta.excerpt: Bringing home a Brussels Griffon puppy means preparing for a sensitive, devoted little dog that will want to be your shadow. This checklist covers the supplies, vet priorities, and socialization essentials for a confident, well-adjusted Griffon.
meta.meta_description: Brussels Griffon puppy checklist: supplies, socialization, training tips, and first-week priorities for this small but big-personality Toy breed.

intro.label: Before Puppy Comes Home
intro.heading: Small Dog, Big Preparation
intro.html:
A Brussels Griffon puppy is small but has significant personality from the very first day. Preparation focuses on creating a safe small-dog environment, sourcing appropriate supplies, and setting up veterinary care with a vet experienced with brachycephalic breeds.

This guide contains affiliate links. As an Amazon Associate, Wooffy earns from qualifying purchases.

Supplies Checklist

  • Small to medium crate — large enough for the adult dog to stand, turn, and lie down comfortably
  • Small-breed food and water bowls (ceramic or stainless, shallow enough for the short muzzle to access easily)
  • Adjustable collar (cat-sized to start) and — importantly — a well-fitted harness for walks (harnesses reduce pressure on the airway in brachycephalic breeds)
  • 4–6 foot lightweight leash
  • ID tag engraved with your phone number
    One option: GoTags Personalized Stainless Steel ID Tag on Amazon. An engraved stainless steel ID tag; you pick the shape and the lines of text at checkout. Put a phone number that's actually answered on it, and update the engraving if you move.
  • High-quality small-breed puppy food (confirm with your breeder)
    One option: Purina Pro Plan Small Breed Puppy, Chicken & Rice (6 lb) on Amazon. Purina Pro Plan's small-breed puppy formula, with kibble sized for small mouths and chicken as the first ingredient. Ask your vet about portions and when to move to adult food.
  • Soft toys and a couple of puzzle feeders for mental enrichment
  • Enzymatic cleaner for accidents
    One option: Rocco & Roxie Enzyme Stain & Odor Eliminator (32 oz) on Amazon. An enzyme stain and odor eliminator for urine, feces and vomit, carrying the Carpet and Rug Institute's seal for carpets. Spot-test on delicate fabrics first.
  • Soft pet facial wipes for daily eye and face cleaning
    One option: Earth Rated Dog Eye Wipes, Unscented (70 ct) on Amazon. Unscented, vet-developed wipes for cleaning dirt and discharge from the fur around the eyes. For cleaning only; persistent staining, redness or discharge is a question for your vet.
  • Small dog dental brush and enzymatic dog toothpaste
    One option: Virbac C.E.T. Enzymatic Toothpaste, Poultry (2.5 oz) on Amazon. A poultry-flavored enzymatic toothpaste made without foaming agents, so it's meant to be swallowed rather than rinsed. Use it with a soft-bristled or finger toothbrush.

Home Safety for a Tiny Dog

  • Brussels Griffon puppies are very small and can be injured by falls — block off stairs with baby gates until the puppy is older and coordinated
  • Secure all spaces where the puppy could get stuck or fall (behind appliances, under furniture gaps, etc.)
  • Ensure all family members — especially children — understand how to handle the puppy gently
  • Remove or secure chewing hazards: electrical cords, small objects that could be swallowed

Vet Setup

  • Find a vet experienced with small and brachycephalic breeds
  • Schedule first wellness exam within 48–72 hours of homecoming
  • Ask about brachycephalic airway assessment — some puppies benefit from early evaluation
  • Discuss dental care schedule — Brussels Griffons need regular professional cleanings and early dental habits matter
  • Enroll in pet insurance immediately

care.label: First Week Setup
care.heading: Settling In a Sensitive Small Dog
care.html:
The Brussels Griffon is emotionally sensitive and will take cues from your energy. The first week should be calm, warm, and structured — not overwhelming.

Day 1–2: Arrival

  • Show the puppy its crate immediately; feed the first meal inside with the door open
  • Establish the house-training schedule: outside after every meal, nap, and play session, and every 1–2 hours otherwise
  • Begin facial cleaning on day one: gently wipe around the eyes and muzzle folds with a soft damp cloth, reward with a tiny treat
  • Keep the first day calm — no overwhelming introduction parties

Day 3–7: Expanding the World

  • Begin short walks on the harness (not collar-only) in the immediate neighborhood
  • Introduce the puppy to 2–3 calm, friendly adults with food rewards
  • Handle feet, ears, and mouth daily to build tolerance for grooming and vet exams
  • Start the dental routine: let the puppy taste the toothpaste, then progress to brief brushing
  • Complete first vet wellness visit

Socialization Focus (Weeks 8–16)

  • Varied adults — this is a breed that can become strongly one-person attached; expose it to many positive human interactions
  • Gentle children (supervised only)
  • Other small dogs in controlled play settings
  • Urban sounds and environments
  • Alone time — gradually increase periods of separation to prevent severe separation anxiety

special.label: Training
special.heading: Training a Sensitive, Opinionated Small Dog
special.html:
The Brussels Griffon is intelligent and can learn quickly, but it is also sensitive and self-directed. Harsh correction is counterproductive — it causes the Griffon to shut down or become defensive. Positive reinforcement with high-value treats and clear, consistent structure is the correct approach.
One option: Blue Buffalo Bits Soft Training Treats, Beef (19 oz) on Amazon. Soft, bite-size training treats with real beef as the first ingredient, small enough for rapid repetitions. Keep treats to about 10% of daily calories.

Priority Training Goals

  • Harness and leash acceptance: Start from day one. The Griffon should walk calmly on a harness — not pull, not refuse to move. Use treats and praise to reward movement alongside you.
  • Sit, stay, come: The basics. Work on them daily in short 3–5 minute sessions. The Griffon's attention span is modest; keep training sessions brief and fun.
  • Alone time training: This is critical for a breed prone to separation anxiety. From day one, create times when the puppy is in its crate with a stuffed Kong while you are home. Gradually extend these periods before ever leaving the house. Do not let the puppy be on your body or following you every minute — independence must be built intentionally.
  • Bite inhibition: Griffon puppies bite. Redirect to toys, say a calm firm "no," and withdraw attention. Never use physical correction on a sensitive small dog.

Things to Avoid

  • Carrying the puppy everywhere — this prevents socialization and builds the dependency that leads to separation anxiety
  • Treating every uncertainty with soothing — comfort-seeking behavior reinforces anxiety. Treat uncertain moments with calm confidence instead.
  • Allowing the puppy to rehearse barking or snapping at visitors — redirect immediately and work on the behavior before it becomes a pattern

faq.q: Are Brussels Griffon puppies hard to house train?
faq.a: Small breeds in general can take longer to fully house train than large breeds, partly due to smaller bladder capacity. The Brussels Griffon is no exception. Consistent scheduling, enzymatic cleaner for accidents, and patience are key. Most Griffons are reliable by 5–6 months with consistent training.

faq.q: Why should I use a harness instead of a collar for my Brussels Griffon?
faq.a: Brachycephalic breeds already have restricted airways. Collar pressure on the neck during pulling can worsen this. A harness distributes pressure across the chest instead, which is safer and more comfortable for breeds with shortened muzzles.

faq.q: How do I prevent separation anxiety in my Brussels Griffon?
faq.a: Start building independence from day one. Create regular alone time in the crate while you are home. Do not allow the puppy to follow you everywhere or be physically on you at all times. Practice calm departures and arrivals. Prevention is much easier than treating established separation anxiety.
